content.title: About
content.content: Whole wheat bread, made from a home recipe or purchased at a bakery, is made from whole wheat grains that are milled into flour and baked into slices. The bread is toasted to a golden crust, enhancing aroma and giving a crunchy texture.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Whole wheat bread contains all parts of the grain – bran, germ, and endosperm – making it more nutritious than white bread.
Toasting triggers the Maillard reaction, creating new flavor compounds that intensify the smell and taste.
Traditional recipes often use a sourdough starter, which improves flavor and increases mineral bioavailability.
In many cultures whole grain bread is a symbol of abundance and health.
Home‑baked bread usually has fewer additives and preservatives than industrially produced loaves.

items.title: Rich in fiber
items.content: Whole grains retain bran, providing both soluble and insoluble fiber that supports healthy digestion.

items.title: Contains B‑vitamins
items.content: Thiamine, niacin, and folate in whole wheat bread aid energy metabolism and nervous system function.

items.title: Source of minerals
items.content: Magnesium, iron, and zinc contribute to metabolism, immunity, and bone health.

items.title: Lower glycemic index
items.content: Compared with white bread, whole wheat raises blood sugar more slowly.

items.title: Promotes satiety
items.content: Fiber and protein help you feel full longer, which can aid weight management.

items.title: Wheat/gluten allergy
items.content: People with wheat allergy or gluten intolerance may experience symptoms after eating whole wheat bread.

items.title: Calorie density
items.content: While nutritious, portion size should be moderated, especially on calorie‑restricted diets.

items.title: Phytic acid content
items.content: Phytates can reduce mineral absorption; soaking or fermenting the dough lowers their level.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Toasted whole wheat bread works well for sandwiches, topped with avocado, cottage cheese, vegetables, or as a side to soups. It can be used as breadcrumbs for casseroles or as a base for croutons.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep the loaf in a paper bag or bread box at room temperature for up to 3 days. For longer storage, freeze slices in an airtight bag and re‑toast as needed.

chicken-or-turkey-noodles-and-vegetables.title: Chicken or Turkey with Noodles, Vegetables and Cheese Sauce

content.title: About
content.content: This dish combines tender chicken or turkey meat, thin noodles, a mix of vegetables (excluding carrots, broccoli, and dark‑green leafy greens) and a creamy cheese sauce. It is rich in protein, carbohydrates and healthy fats, as well as vitamins and minerals supplied by the vegetables.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Chicken and turkey are among the most popular sources of lean protein worldwide.
Noodles made from durum wheat provide lasting satiety.
Cheese sauce is often prepared from cream cheese and milk, giving it a smooth, savory flavor.
Vegetables such as bell pepper, zucchini and peas add bright color and a crunchy texture.
The recipe can be easily adapted to different tastes by swapping the meat for plant‑based alternatives.

items.title: High‑quality protein
items.content: Chicken and turkey contain all essential amino acids, supporting muscle growth and tissue repair.

items.title: Energy‑providing carbs
items.content: Noodles supply quick‑release carbohydrates needed for physical activity.

items.title: Vitamins and minerals
items.content: The vegetables contribute vitamin C, vitamin A and potassium, which aid immunity and heart function.

items.title: Calcium from cheese sauce
items.content: The cheese sauce is a good source of calcium, important for bone and dental health.

items.title: Moderate saturated fat
items.content: Using low‑fat cheese and a modest amount of oil keeps saturated fat levels moderate.

items.title: Dairy allergy
items.content: Cheese sauce may trigger reactions in people with lactose intolerance or milk allergy.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: Prepared cheese sauce can be high in salt; monitor the amount added.

items.title: Processed meat additives
items.content: If using pre‑cooked chicken or turkey pieces, check for preservatives and additives.

items.title: Food safety
items.content: Meat must be cooked thoroughly to avoid food‑borne illness.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the dish hot, tossing the noodles with meat, vegetables and cheese sauce. Garnish with fresh herbs such as parsley or dill and a pinch of black pepper for extra aroma.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store leftovers in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 2 days. When reheating, add a splash of milk or water to keep the sauce from becoming too thick.

content.title: About
content.content: Spaghetti Sauce with Seafood is a ready‑to‑use tomato sauce enriched with pieces of shrimp, mussels, calamari and fish. It is perfect for quick pasta, risotto or seafood dishes. The flavor combines the sweetness of tomatoes, a hint of garlic heat and the aroma of fresh marine delicacies.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Tomatoes in the sauce undergo a short heat treatment to retain most of their vitamins.
Seafood pieces are usually pre‑seared, which intensifies their aroma.
In Italy similar sauces are called "sugo di mare" and are used in traditional coastal recipes.
The sauce may contain a small amount of white wine, adding depth to the taste.
Because natural ingredients are used, no artificial flavorings are required.

items.title: Rich in omega‑3 fatty acids
items.content: Seafood provides omega‑3s that support heart and vascular health.

items.title: High protein content
items.content: Shrimp, mussels and fish supply a complete set of amino acids beneficial for muscles and tissue repair.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Seafood is a source of vitamin B12 and niacin, important for the nervous system and metabolism.

items.title: Lycopene in tomatoes
items.content: Tomatoes are rich in lycopene, an antioxidant that may reduce the risk of certain chronic diseases.

items.title: Low in saturated fat
items.content: Unlike cream‑based sauces, this product contains minimal saturated fat.

items.title: Seafood allergy
items.content: The product can trigger allergic reactions in individuals sensitive to crustaceans or mollusks.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: The sauce can be salty; people limiting sodium intake should monitor portion size.

items.title: Glutamate presence
items.content: Some recipes include added monosodium glutamate, which may cause sensitivity in certain consumers.

items.title: Post‑opening storage
items.content: After opening, keep the sauce refrigerated and consume within 3‑5 days.

content.title: How to Use
content.content: Heat the sauce in a pan, add cooked spaghetti and stir. You can also toss in extra fresh seafood, herbs (parsley, basil) and a drizzle of olive oil. The sauce works well for casseroles, lasagna or as a base for risotto.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store the unopened sauce in a cool, dry place. Once opened, keep it in the refrigerator in an airtight container. Discard if the smell, color or texture changes or if mold appears.

squash-summer-casserole-with-cheese-sauc.title: Summer Squash Casserole with Cheese Sauce

content.title: About
content.content: Summer squash casserole with cheese sauce is a dish made from tender pieces of squash baked in a casserole dish and topped with a creamy cheese sauce. The combination of sweet squash and rich cheese makes it a popular side or a light main course.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Summer squash (Cucurbita pepo) ripens in warm months and has a softer flesh than winter varieties.
Cheese sauce is often prepared from cream cheese, milk, and spices, giving the dish a smooth flavor.
Squash casseroles are traditional in Mediterranean and Eastern European cuisines.
Squash is high in beta‑carotene, which the body converts to vitamin A.
The recipe can be easily adapted for vegetarians by using plant‑based cheese alternatives.

items.title: Rich in vitamin A
items.content: Squash provides beta‑carotene, supporting vision, immune function, and skin health.

items.title: Low in calories
items.content: 100 g of squash contains about 20 kcal, making the dish suitable for calorie‑controlled diets.

items.title: Source of dietary fiber
items.content: Fiber aids digestion and promotes a feeling of fullness.

items.title: Calcium from cheese
items.content: The cheese sauce adds calcium, essential for strong bones and teeth.

items.title: Antioxidants
items.content: Squash contains vitamin C and other antioxidants that protect cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Dairy allergy
items.content: The cheese sauce may trigger reactions in people with lactose intolerance or milk allergy.

items.title: High sodium content
items.content: Prepared cheese sauces often contain salt; individuals with hypertension should monitor portion size.

items.title: Potential foodborne illness
items.content: Squash should be fully cooked; raw or undercooked squash can be hard to digest.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the casserole hot as a side to meat or fish, or enjoy it as a standalone dish. Garnish with fresh herbs, nuts, or seeds for extra crunch if desired.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep the cooked casserole in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 3‑4 days. Reheat in the oven or microwave at 180 °C until the top is lightly browned.
